record.title: Unit 42 reports prompt-injection credential exposure in a tested AWS AgentCore Harness setup
record.summary: On September 18, 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 published a technical report describing a controlled SupportCo simulation using AWS AgentCore Harness. Unit 42 reports that an indirect prompt injection could steer the default shell tool in its tested setup to expose an operator service credential that AgentCore Identity had resolved for a downstream MCP service; the researchers say they replayed that credential against their simulated service. AWS documentation confirms that shell and file_operations are available unless restricted with allowedTools, which scopes tool selection at InvokeHarness, and documents per-session microVM isolation and customer responsibility for input validation. Unit 42 says AWS closed its May disclosure as informative on June 10 under shared responsibility, citing customer-side controls. That disposition is not independently confirmed here. No independent reproduction, customer incident or prevalence estimate was inspected; the public account supports a bounded source-reported test, not a general AWS vulnerability or population-risk claim.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Unit 42 reports that, in its controlled SupportCo simulation, indirect prompt injection could steer the AgentCore Harness shell to expose an operator service credential resolved for a downstream MCP integration, which the researchers then replayed against their simulated service. This is one source-reported configuration, not evidence of a customer incident or widespread exposure.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: AWS documentation states that shell and file_operations are available in every session unless restricted with allowedTools, and that allowedTools scopes model tool selection at InvokeHarness. The documentation also describes per-session microVM isolation and customer responsibility for input validation and prompt-injection prevention.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Unit 42 says AWS closed its June 10 disclosure as informative under the shared responsibility model, citing allowedTools scoping and egress filtering as customer-side controls; no direct AWS case response or public AWS statement was inspected.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent test has reproduced Unit 42’s credential exposure in the reported configuration.
The June 10 AWS closure as informative is reported by Unit 42; no direct AWS response, advisory or versioned status change was inspected.
The report does not establish how many deployments use the relevant configuration or whether customers were exposed.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproducible, this changes security architecture choices for managed-agent runtimes that resolve downstream credentials while exposing a default general-purpose shell. The potential impact spans credential boundary design and deployment review; the score does not imply prevalence, customer compromise or an AWS-confirmed vulnerability.
limitations: The development records a bounded Unit 42 source-reported simulation, not an independently reproduced vulnerability or an AWS-confirmed security status.
No actual customer exposure, prevalence or exploit activity was demonstrated in the inspected material.
The source author sells security products and related services; its impact and mitigation framing warrants independent scrutiny.

Unit 42 reports that an indirect prompt injection could steer the default shell tool in its tested setup to expose an operator service credential that AgentCore Identity had resolved for a downstream MCP service; the researchers say they replayed that credential against their simulated service. AWS documentation confirms that shell and file_operations are available unless restricted with allowedTools, which scopes tool selection at InvokeHarness, and documents per-session microVM isolation and customer responsibility for input validation. Unit 42 says AWS closed its May disclosure as informative on June 10 under shared responsibility, citing customer-side controls. That disposition is not independently confirmed here. technical.claimed_result: Unit 42 reports successful credential exposure and replay in its simulated SupportCo setup, and says AWS closed its disclosure as informative on June 10. Neither the specific behavior nor the closure outcome was independently confirmed in this activation.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public Unit 42 report documents its controlled test procedure and reports credential exposure and replay against a simulated downstream service. AWS documentation independently confirms default tool availability and the documented permission/shared-responsibility model. the research desk did not execute the test or reproduce the reported credential exposure.
technical.implementation_status: Unit 42 disclosed the finding to AWS on May 19, 2026 and reports AWS closed it as informative on June 10, 2026. AWS documentation continues to describe default built-in tools and allowedTools restrictions in the inspected current guide. No direct vendor status statement or versioned remediation record was located.
technical.mechanism: Unit 42 describes a managed harness session with a downstream MCP integration whose service credential is resolved by AgentCore Identity for use by the harness. In its simulated configuration, the built-in shell ran in the same session context and was steered through indirect prompt injection. The report says this let the researchers expose and replay the simulated operator credential. AWS documentation confirms default shell availability unless restricted and documents microVM isolation at session level; it does not independently verify the report’s same-session memory-access result.
technical.regime: One Unit 42-created simulated support workflow on AWS AgentCore Harness with a configured downstream MCP server and an AgentCore Identity credential. The report says its test used a default shell configuration; exact affected service version, deployment prevalence and current behavior are not independently established.
technical.reproducibility: The report provides an end-to-end account and test artifacts in its figures, but the research desk did not run the experiment and located no independent reproduction. Reproduction should use a non-customer isolated harness and synthetic downstream credentials/data.
technical.strongest_baseline: AWS documentation states that shell and file_operations are available in each session unless restricted, and that allowedTools controls model tool selection at InvokeHarness. It describes sessions as isolated microVMs and assigns customers responsibility for input validation and prompt-injection prevention. This is the documented configuration baseline, not an evaluation of the reported attack path.

brief.title: Unit 42 reports prompt-injection credential exposure in a tested AWS AgentCore Harness setup
brief.why_it_matters: If the report is reproducible under the documented configuration, it shows that credential-vault encryption at rest and in transit does not by itself bound what a default shell tool can access after a credential is resolved for a downstream call. Managed-agent security reviews should distinguish caller permission to invoke a harness from the authority and in-process access granted to tools inside that harness. The report is one vendor’s controlled demonstration, with no independent reproduction or evidence of customer exposure.
